solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Have no mercy hiding spitefulness

indicators.note: something that hides another holds it concealed inside itself, so the letters sit within the run of words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A ruthless person shows no mercy while concealing their malice.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer spans haVE NO Mercy; the surface makes 'hiding' sound like a beating.
explanation.definitionFit: Venom is used figuratively for bitter malice or spite in speech and behaviour.

clue.text: Enjoy an e-cigarette with clumsy fellow after 5

indicators.note: coming after sets the order: the second item is placed behind the first

parts.note: V is the Roman numeral for five
an ape is a big, clumsy, oafish man

explanation.surface: Someone lights up an e-cigarette alongside an awkward friend at five o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: The '5' looks like a time of day but is the Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: To vape is to inhale vapour from an electronic cigarette, the modern substitute for smoking tobacco.

clue.text: Awesome element of drone attack

indicators.note: an element is one component within a larger whole, so the letters are a part of the phrase

parts.note: the letters straddle the join between the two words

explanation.surface: Someone admires a strike carried out by unmanned aircraft.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits in droNE ATtack.
explanation.definitionFit: Neat is informal, chiefly American, slang for excellent or cool, the same enthusiastic sense as awesome.

clue.text: Pop singer tucking into Beck's cake

indicators.note: to tuck into a place is to slip inside it, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: Beck is the setter, so the setter's is 'mine'
Adele is the British pop singer

explanation.surface: A pop star greedily eating a cake belonging to someone called Beck.
explanation.walkthrough: Beck is this puzzle's setter, and setters often refer to themselves by name, so the possessive stands for the first-person 'belonging to me'.
explanation.definitionFit: A madeleine is a small, shell-shaped French sponge baked in a scalloped mould, made famous by Proust.

clue.text: Pop singer's praise set back International Publishers' Association

indicators.note: setting something back moves it rearward, so the word is read from its end

parts.note: to laud is to praise
the initials of the organisation

explanation.surface: A singer's acclaim is delayed by a trade body for publishers.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive on 'singer's' is a joining 's (singer is), leaving 'Pop singer' as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Dua Lipa is a British-Albanian pop star known for hits such as New Rules and Levitating.

clue.text: Changing one or the other initially to show hesitation

indicators.note: changing something swaps part of it for something else
initially points to the beginning, so the swap happens at the opening letter only

parts.note: either means one or the other of two

explanation.surface: Wavering between two options, someone hesitates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' says only the first letter of EITHER changes; the new letter is not clued, so it comes from the definition and crossers.
explanation.definitionFit: To dither is to be indecisive and waver, unable to make up your mind.

clue.text: Cut taxes without limits

indicators.note: the limits of a word are its two ends, so without them only the inside stays

parts.note: drop the first and last letters

explanation.surface: A call to slash taxation with no ceiling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut taxes' reads as a policy; the definition is 'Cut' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: To axe spending or jobs is to cut them drastically, a common newspaper verb.

clue.text: Complete rearrangement of triangle

indicators.note: a rearrangement puts the same items in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A geometry exercise: fully redrawing a three-sided shape.
explanation.walkthrough: The mathematical surface also hints at the calculus sense of the answer, but the meaning needed is 'whole'.
explanation.definitionFit: Integral means whole or entire, with all necessary parts present, as in an integral design.

clue.text: Cry about being trapped in distant back street

indicators.note: something trapped in a place is held inside it

parts.note: far off, away

indicators.note: about can mean turned around, so the word faces the other way

parts.note: to yell is to cry out

explanation.surface: Someone shouts about being cornered in a remote alley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'concerning' but is the turnaround signal, and 'distant' is the outer piece rather than describing the street.
explanation.definitionFit: An alleyway is a narrow passage between buildings, the same as a back street or lane.

clue.text: Enthusiastic approval of profit and loss review by accountant

parts.note: P and L abbreviate profit and loss, as in a P&L account
an audit is an accountant's inspection of the books

explanation.surface: An accountant's glowing report on the profit and loss figures.
explanation.walkthrough: P&L is the standard abbreviation for a profit and loss statement.
explanation.definitionFit: A plaudit is an expression of praise or applause, usually heard in the plural.

clue.text: Praise bygone tax deducting just one pound

parts.note: ex means former

indicators.note: deducting takes an amount away, so something is subtracted

parts.note: a toll is a charge or levy
L is the abbreviation for a pound; TOLL has two, and only one goes

explanation.surface: Praising an old tax that took only a single pound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just one' matters: TOLL loses only one of its two Ls.
explanation.definitionFit: To extol is to praise highly and enthusiastically, a formal verb for lauding.

clue.text: Leave feeling excitement for just a moment

parts.note: to flee is to leave in haste
tingly describes a thrilled, prickling sensation

explanation.surface: Someone departs with a brief thrill of excitement.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is an adverbial phrase at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Fleetingly means briefly, in a passing way that lasts only an instant.

clue.text: Plastic on sidecar coated with metal

indicators.note: plastic material can be moulded into any shape, so the letters are reshaped

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A motorcycle sidecar has plastic panels, yet is plated in metal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plastic' reads as a material, contrasting with metal, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something iron-cased is enclosed in a shell of iron, so it is covered with a metal skin.

clue.text: Modifying giant pad in an unusual way

indicators.note: done unusually means not in the normal order, so the letters are arranged differently

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone customising an enormous notepad or cushion in an odd fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Modifying' could be grammatical, qualifying 'giant pad', but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Adapting means altering something to suit a new use or condition, much like changing it.

clue.text: Started directly below track

parts.note: under means beneath
a way is a path or track

explanation.surface: Something began just beneath a railway line or path.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry, 'directly below' also describes placing one piece over the next.
explanation.definitionFit: A project that is underway has begun and is now in progress.

clue.text: Man strayed to the west

indicators.note: in an across entry, heading west means travelling right to left, the opposite of reading order

parts.note: to stray morally is to sin

explanation.surface: A man wandered off westward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strayed' suggests wandering geographically, but it means went wrong morally.
explanation.definitionFit: Dennis is a common male first name, so any man could be so called.

clue.text: Child attending a part of recital

parts.note: a son is a male child
to be at an event is to attend it
taken as written

explanation.surface: A youngster goes along to a portion of a concert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A' belongs to the wordplay, leaving 'part of recital' as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A sonata is an instrumental composition, typically for piano or a soloist, often played as one item in a recital programme.

clue.text: Heartless, reckless pause in proceedings

indicators.note: without a heart means the central part is taken out

parts.note: taken as written; its middle two letters go

explanation.surface: A cruel, rash break in some meeting or trial.
explanation.walkthrough: RECKLESS has eight letters, so its heart is the middle pair KL.
explanation.definitionFit: A recess is a break in the sittings of a court or parliament, a temporary halt in business.

clue.text: Favourite source of personal recommendation

indicators.note: the source of something is where it starts, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: its first letter
a reference is a written recommendation, as for a job

explanation.surface: A favoured way to find a personal endorsement.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a reference is the letter a former employer writes to recommend someone.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun, your favourite thing is your top choice, the one you like best among options.

clue.text: Mailed out in absentia

indicators.note: in says the letters are contained within the following word

parts.note: the middle letters of the word

explanation.surface: A letter was posted while its recipient was not present.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In absentia' is a Latin phrase meaning in someone's absence; 'in' does double duty in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Something mailed out has been posted or dispatched to its recipient.

clue.text: Nervous editor going crazy ultimately

parts.note: ED is the usual abbreviation for editor

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so only closing letters are taken

parts.note: the last letter of each word

explanation.surface: An anxious editor finally loses their mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ultimately' reads as 'in the end', but it takes the final letters of both words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Edgy means tense, anxious and on edge.

clue.text: Statesman from Isle of Wight area, close to Sandown

parts.note: IOW is the abbreviation for the Isle of Wight, an island county off England's south coast
A is the abbreviation for area

indicators.note: the close of something is its end, so the final letter is taken

parts.note: its final letter

explanation.surface: A politician from the Isle of Wight, near the resort of Sandown.
explanation.walkthrough: Sandown is a seaside town on the Isle of Wight; 'Statesman' is not a politician but a person from a US state.
explanation.definitionFit: An Iowan lives in Iowa, one of the American states, so is playfully a man of a state.

clue.text: Once-called dictator's opposing vote

indicators.note: a dictator here is someone dictating words to be written down, so the word is spoken

parts.note: a no vote, spoken with the vowel said the French way

explanation.surface: A former tyrant casts a vote against.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dictator' suggests a tyrant but means someone speaking for a secretary; NAY sounds like the answer in its French pronunciation 'nay'.
explanation.definitionFit: Née introduces a woman's former or maiden name, the name she was once called by.

clue.text: Dean set off for area of London

indicators.note: off can mean wrong or not right, so the letters are out of their proper order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A college dean departs for a district of the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is 'Dean set', with 'off' the signal: 'set off' reads as a phrase but splits.
explanation.definitionFit: The East End is the traditionally working-class district of east London, home of cockneys.

clue.text: "They let off steam", blokes said

indicators.note: said means spoken, so the word is judged by how it is pronounced

parts.note: geezer is British slang for a man; bloke is British for a chap

explanation.surface: Some men remark on people venting their frustration.
explanation.walkthrough: In British English the answer is pronounced 'geezers'; 'let off steam' also means venting anger.
explanation.definitionFit: Geysers are hot springs that periodically shoot water and vapour into the air.

clue.text: Rather eccentric nickname for a girl

definitions.meaning: first meaning: slightly mad or odd
second meaning: a pet form of Dorothy

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests an odd pet name; the two parts are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is British informal for mildly crazy and also a diminutive of the girl's name Dorothy.
